## Paper vs Digital Note-Taking: Research & Trade-Offs | Notsu
The headline finding: laptop note-takers tended to transcribe lectures nearly verbatim, while longhand note-takers — unable to write as fast as they could type — were forced to process, summarize, and reframe as they wrote. On factual recall questions the two groups performed similarly. On conceptual questions, the longhand group did better, even when laptop users were explicitly told not to transcribe verbatim, and even when both groups were allowed to review their notes before testing. [...] The short answer: The best available evidence favors handwriting on paper for learning and retention. Longhand note-takers tend to do better on conceptual questions than laptop note-takers (Mueller & Oppenheimer, 2014), and brain-imaging work shows handwriting produces more extensive neural connectivity than typing (Van der Weel & Van der Meer, 2024). plan.title: Meet Your Notes Again: A New Note-Taking App
plan.description: A launch video for a note-taking app built around the moment between writing and finding. It shows why notes get lost, what people want from their tools, and how one app fixes it.

beats.narration: Think of the last great idea you wrote down. Now try to find it. Three months later, 62% of people say they spend too much time searching for information.

props.label: say they spend too much time searching for information

beats.speaker: narrator

beats.narration: Here is why. Every two minutes, a meeting, an email or a ping interrupts your work. So the note lands in whichever app happens to be open.

clip_queries: person checking phone notifications at desk
props.alt: people working in open plan office

beats.narration: Note apps fail between writing and retrieving. Capturing is easy. Finding it again later is where ideas go to disappear.
So what do people actually want? Professionals were asked what drives their choice of digital note tools. The answer was not fancy features. Ease of use came first.

props.text: Ease of use matters more than any feature.

beats.narration: Ease of use was chosen by 35%. Cloud sync followed at 25%. Time savings reached 20%, smart features 12%, and collaboration 8%.
Our rule is simple. If opening the app takes longer than grabbing a notebook, you will reach for the notebook.

clip_queries: typing on laptop at coffee shop

beats.narration: Meet your new notes app. It is built around three things: capturing ideas, finding them again, and turning them into action.

props.title: Meet your notes, found again
props.subtitle: Capture fast. Find anything. Act on it.

beats.narration: First, capture. Jot down your idea. Second, search. Find it again later. Third, act. Turn notes into next steps.

steps.label: Capture
steps.detail: Type or write by hand, instantly

beats.narration: AI can help with the boring part. You are not alone in this: 19% of employees already use AI tools to take notes at work.

props.label: 19% of employees use AI tools to take notes
props.title: AI note-taking at work

beats.narration: Among Gen Z employees, 43% use AI note-taking tools. For millennials, it is around 30%. The habit is growing fast, and people want it built in.

props.title: Use AI note tools at work

beats.narration: The whole market is growing too. Note-taking is expected to reach 38.65 billion dollars by 2035, at 8.4% growth a year. People are choosing better tools.
Writing by hand has a real edge for learning. Longhand note-takers did better on conceptual questions, because they had to process ideas.
Whether you work in a team, study, or just collect ideas, your notes are there when you need them.
Stop losing your best ideas. Download the app today and find your next great idea exactly when you need it.

props.text: Write it once. Find it forever.

mismatch_scenes: beat 3 (diagram): its narration never says ['Write', 'Lost in the pile', 'Retrieve']

accuracy.reason: Most stats trace to the notes, but they are misapplied: the 62% figure is framed as a note-retrieval problem, and the market figure is said to show 'people are choosing better tools'. The script also implies features (handwriting, plain-words search) as if they were real.

coverage.reason: It has a problem-solution-benefit arc and a call to action, but the stat-heavy middle (beats 9-11) is filler. It names no concrete product details or placeholders, and the notes' competitor and market context goes unused.

structure.reason: The chapter order is clear. But the market stats in beats 9-11 interrupt the pitch, and the handwriting section (beat 12) arrives after the app is introduced and undercuts a typing-first product.

hook_ending.reason: The opening 'Think of the last great idea you wrote down. Now try to find it.' is engaging. The ending 'Write it once. Find it forever.' lands, though the call to action is generic.

tone.reason: Conversational, promotional and fitting for a launch video, with only a few stiff stat-reading moments.

visuals.reason: Scene types vary well, and the charts show real numbers that match the narration. The stock clip queries are generic, and the versus scene contradicts the product pitch.

originality.reason: The notebook-versus-app line is a good touch, but the video leans on generic stat dumps and cliches like 'ideas go to disappear'.

instructions.reason: The length is about right and there is a CTA. But the app's features are invented without being flagged as placeholders, and the app has no name.

language.reason: Fluent, clean English with short sentences. A few are slightly clumsy, such as 'Our rule is simple'.
